<timestamp>Thursday, May 21, 2026, 2:43 PM (UTC+8)</timestamp>
<user_query>
Definition (Pure strategy in dynamic games)
We let 𝐼 = {ℎ𝑖(𝑥): 𝑥 ∈ 𝑁𝑖} be a collection of possible information sets of
player 𝑖 and 𝑆𝑖 be the strategic set of player 𝑖. A player 𝑖’s pure strategy
is defined as a function 𝑠𝑖: 𝐼 → 𝑆𝑖 which assigns a single strategy in 𝑆𝑖 to
every information set ℎ𝑖(⋅) ∈ 𝐼.

Explain this more carefully
</user_query>

The definition has several layers. Let me break it down step by step.

---

## The key idea

In a **dynamic game**, a player doesn't just pick a single action. Instead, the player must plan for **multiple possible situations** they might face. A pure strategy is that complete plan.

---

## Breaking down the notation

### 1. Information sets $I = \{h_i(x) : x \in N_i\}$

Recall that $N_i$ is the set of all nodes where player $i$ must make a decision. Since player $i$ may not know exactly which node they are at, nodes that look the same to them are grouped together into an **information set** $h_i(x)$.

Collecting all such information sets gives you $I$ — the set of all possible "situations" player $i$ might find themselves in.

### 2. The strategic set $S_i$

This is just the set of **actions available** to player $i$ at each decision point. For example, in the Battle of the Sexes game, $S_i = \{B, M\}$.

### 3. The function $s_i : I \to S_i$

This says: **for every possible situation** (information set) $h_i(\cdot) \in I$, the strategy $s_i$ assigns **exactly one action** from $S_i$.

---

## Why this matters

### Example: Battle of the Sexes (perfect information version)

Player 2 (Girl) moves **first** and **knows** her own choice. Her only information set is a single node:

$$I_{\text{Girl}} = \{\{x_1\}\}$$

Her strategy is just one action:

$$s_{\text{Girl}} = s_2(\{x_1\}) \in \{B, M\}$$

Player 1 (Boy) moves **second** and **does not know** what the Girl chose. He has **two** information sets:

$$I_{\text{Boy}} = \{\{x_1\}, \{x_2\}\}$$

So his strategy must specify what to do **in each case**:

$$s_{\text{Boy}} = \left(s_1(\{x_1\}), \; s_1(\{x_2\})\right) \in \{B, M\} \times \{B, M\}$$

That is, $s_1$ is an **ordered pair** like $(B, M)$ — meaning "if I think the Girl chose $B$, I pick $B$; if I think she chose $M$, I pick $M$."

### The consistency rule

There's one crucial constraint:

> If two nodes belong to the **same information set** (the player cannot distinguish them), the strategy **must assign the same action** to both.

This is written as: if $h_i(x) = h_i(x')$, then $s_i(h_i(x)) = s_i(h_i(x'))$.

It makes intuitive sense — if you can't tell two situations apart, you can't act differently in them.

---

## Summary

| Component | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $I$ | All possible "situations" player $i$ might face |
| $S_i$ | Actions available to player $i$ |
| $s_i : I \to S_i$ | A **complete plan**: for every situation, specify exactly one action |

The strategy is essentially a **contingency plan** — it tells the player exactly what to do at every point in the game, for every scenario they might encounter based on what they know.

<timestamp>Thursday, May 21, 2026, 3:37 PM (UTC+8)</timestamp>
<user_query>
For all information set, the action set of all the elements are the same
</user_query>

Yes, this is a **fundamental consistency condition** for information sets. Let me explain why this must always hold.

---

## The condition

For any information set $h$ belonging to player $i$, **all nodes** $x \in h$ must have the **same available action set**:

$$A_i(x) = A_i(x') \quad \text{for all } x, x' \in h$$

---

## Why must this be true?

The core idea is: **if a player cannot distinguish two nodes, they must face the same choices at those nodes.**

Consider two nodes $x$ and $x'$ in the same information set $h_i(x) = h_i(x')$.

- Player $i$ is at $x$ **or** $x'$, but **cannot tell which**.
- If the action sets were different — say $A_i(x) = \{H, M\}$ but $A_i(x') = \{L\}$ — then the player could **infer** which node they are at simply by observing their available choices.
- That would **contradict** the definition of an information set, which groups together nodes that the player **genuinely cannot distinguish**.

So the information set itself **must encode** which actions are available. Every node in the same information set has the same action set by definition.

---

## Example: Penalty Kick (imperfect information)

Goalkeeper (Player 2) has three information sets at the first round:

$$h_2(x_1^{(2)}) = h_2(x_2^{(2)}) = h_2(x_3^{(2)}) = \{x_1^{(2)}, x_2^{(2)}, x_3^{(2)}\}$$

At **each** of these nodes, the goalkeeper has the **same** action set:

$$A_2 = \{L, M, R\} \quad \text{(jump Left, stay Middle, jump Right)}$$

regardless of which node they are at. The goalkeeper cannot know which direction the kicker chose, so from their perspective, all three nodes feel identical — same three actions, same situation.

---

## Contrast: Battle of the Sexes (perfect information)

Player 1 (Boy) has **one** information set containing **one** node:

$$h_1(x_1^{(2)}) = \{x_1^{(2)}\}$$

His action set is:

$$A_1 = \{B, M\}$$

Player 2 (Girl) also has one information set with one node:

$$h_2(x_1^{(1)}) = \{x_1^{(1)}\}$$

Her action set is:

$$A_2 = \{B, M\}$$

Because each information set contains only a single node, the condition is trivially satisfied.

---

## Summary

The condition "all elements in an information set have the same action set" is not an extra assumption — it is **built into** the definition of an information set. It ensures the information set represents a situation where the player genuinely cannot gather any more information, and therefore the available choices must be the same.

<timestamp>Thursday, May 21, 2026, 3:38 PM (UTC+8)</timestamp>
<user_query>
Sequential rationality, can you explain the notation Vi(si;s-i)|_h_i(x)
</user_query>

## Breaking down the notation

$$V_i(s_i; s_{-i})|_{h_i(x)}$$

This notation means: **player $i$'s payoff when the game reaches information set $h_i(x)$, given that player $i$ follows strategy $s_i$ and all other players follow $s_{-i}$.**

---

### 1. $V_i(s_i; s_{-i})$ — the payoff function

This is player $i$'s total payoff under a particular strategy profile $(s_i, s_{-i})$.

- $s_i$ is player $i$'s strategy
- $s_{-i}$ is shorthand for "all other players' strategies" $(s_1, \ldots, s_{i-1}, s_{i+1}, \ldots, s_n)$

### 2. $|_{h_i(x)}$ — conditioning on an information set

The vertical bar with $h_i(x)$ means **"evaluated at the point where the game reaches information set $h_i(x)$."**

In a dynamic game, the full strategy profile $(s_i, s_{-i})$ determines what happens **at every stage**. The notation $|_{h_i(x)}$ lets us zoom in and ask:

> **"What is player $i$'s payoff if we only look at the subgame starting from $h_i(x)$, assuming all players follow $(s_i, s_{-i})$?"**

---

## Why is this notation needed?

The key is that $V_i(s_i; s_{-i})$ normally represents the **total payoff** from the **entire** game. But in sequential rationality, we want to check whether a player is playing **optimally at every stage** — not just overall.

The $|_{h_i(x)}$ restriction lets us evaluate the payoff **from that point onward**, not the whole game.

---

## How it works in practice

Consider the Battle of the Sexes (perfect information). Player 1 (Boy) has two information sets:

$$h_1(x_1^{(2)}) = \{x_1^{(2)}\}, \quad h_1(x_2^{(2)}) = \{x_2^{(2)}\}$$

At information set $h_1(x_1^{(2)})$, the Boy knows the Girl chose $B$. The payoff from this point onward is:

$$V_1(s_1; s_2)|_{h_1(x_1^{(2)})}$$

If both players follow the strategy profile $((B, M), B)$ — meaning the Boy plays $(B, M)$ (picks $B$ at $h_1(x_1^{(2)})$ and $M$ at $h_1(x_2^{(2)})$), and the Girl plays $B$ — then:

$$V_1(s_1; s_2)|_{h_1(x_1^{(2)})} = 4$$

This is the payoff **conditional on reaching the $B$ node**. The Boy gets 4 because the game proceeds along the path $B \to B$.

At the other information set:

$$V_1(s_1; s_2)|_{h_1(x_2^{(2)})} = -3$$

---

## Sequential rationality in notation

Recall the definition of sequential rationality for player $i$:

$$V_i(s_i^*; s_{-i}^*)|_{h_i(x)} \geq V_i(s_i; s_{-i}^*)|_{h_i(x)} \quad \text{for all } h_i(x) \text{ and all } s_i$$

This says: **at every information set $h_i(x)$, player $i$'s chosen strategy $s_i^*$ yields a payoff at least as good as any alternative strategy $s_i$, given that all other players stick to $s_{-i}^*$.**

The payoff is evaluated **locally** at each information set — not the total game payoff.

---

## Summary

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $V_i$ | Player $i$'s payoff function |
| $s_i$ | Player $i$'s strategy |
| $s_{-i}$ | All other players' strategies |
| $|_{h_i(x)}$ | Restrict evaluation to the subgame starting from information set $h_i(x)$ |
| **Together** | "Player $i$'s payoff at information set $h_i(x)$, given everyone follows $(s_i, s_{-i})$" |

The $|_{h_i(x)}$ restriction is what makes sequential rationality **stronger** than Nash equilibrium — it requires optimal play **at every** information set, not just in equilibrium.

<timestamp>Thursday, May 21, 2026, 3:39 PM (UTC+8)</timestamp>
<user_query>
so it's a restriction to the subforest where the root nodes are the information set.
</user_query>

Exactly right. Think of the game tree as a rooted tree with the initial node as the root. When you restrict to an information set $h_i(x)$, you're essentially looking at the **subtree(s) rooted at each node in that information set**.

More precisely:

- An information set $h_i(x)$ contains one or more nodes.
- Each node $x' \in h_i(x)$ is the **root of a subtree** — the game continues downward from $x'$ following the strategies $(s_i, s_{-i})$.
- The restriction $|_{h_i(x)}$ evaluates the payoff by looking at **all these subtrees**, weighted by the player's beliefs about which node they are at.

Since the player cannot distinguish between nodes in the same information set, and because all nodes in an information set have the same action set and lead to isomorphic subtrees (same structure, possibly different payoffs), this is effectively like taking the **union of subtrees** rooted at $h_i(x)$.

In the special case of **perfect information**, each information set contains exactly one node, so it's just a single subtree. In **imperfect information**, you have multiple root nodes (a "forest"), and the player evaluates the payoff based on their beliefs about which node they're at.

So yes — your intuition of a "subforest rooted at the information set" is a clean way to think about it.
